title: Dakuwa Aya
author: Iquo Bassey
desc: Tiger nut dry-fried five to ten minutes until it browns, pounded to powder, bound with groundnut paste and honey into balls.
longDesc: Dakuwa is the northern sweet snack and this is the tiger nut version rather than the more usual groundnut one. A cup of very dried tiger nut is washed, sun-dried, then dry-fried for five to ten minutes until it starts browning, cooled and pounded to a powder. Half a cup of roasted groundnut is blended smooth with dried pepper and ginger, mixed into the aya powder, and half to three quarters of a cup of honey binds the whole thing into a ball that is wrapped and then moulded into small pieces to serve. Cloves are in it, which is unusual in this region.
ingredients: 1 cup very dried tiger nut powder
equipment: Mortar and pestle, or a blender
steps: Wash the tiger nut and sun-dry it.
Dry-fry it until it starts browning, 5 to 10 minutes, then cool and pound or blend it to a powder.
Blend the groundnut, the pepper and the ginger into a smooth paste.
Mix the aya powder with the groundnut blend.
Add the honey and knead it into a ball. Wrap in foil if you are storing it whole.
Store in a container at room temperature.
Mould into small balls to serve.
chefTips: Very dried tiger nut, and the source says so twice. Any moisture at all and the powder will not keep and the dakuwa will not hold.
Until it starts browning is the frying cue, at five to ten minutes. Tiger nut goes from pale to burnt quickly.
Cool it completely before pounding. Warm tiger nut goes oily in the mortar rather than powdering.
Honey to taste within the half-to-three-quarters range. Less gives a crumblier dakuwa, more a chewier one.
Knead it as one ball and wrap it, then mould pieces as you need them. It keeps better whole.
This is dakuwa aya, the tiger nut version. Standard groundnut dakuwa could not be found from any citable named source and is not published here.
It is one of only two recipes in this entire northern set containing cloves — the other being a yaji variant its own author flags as a deviation.
commonMistakes: Using tiger nut that is not thoroughly dried.
Adding all the honey at once without testing the texture.
Moulding it all into small balls at the start, which dries them out.
sources: Adapted from 'How to make Dakuwa Aya', byline '1Qfoodplatter'. Local name as printed: Dakuwa Aya, a 'Northern Nigerian sweet snack'. Headnote as printed: 'If there is something that my northern country men do not lack is the abundance of snacks and sweet ones at that.'

Quantities exactly as printed: 1 cup very dried Tiger nut powder; 1/2 cup ground roasted Ground nut; Dried Pepper to taste; 1/2 teaspoon Cloves; Half teaspoon ginger powder; 1/2 – 3/4 cup Honey. Yield not specified, and no doneness cue beyond 'until browning' for the dry-frying step.

Method as printed: wash and sun-dry the tiger nut; dry fry until browning (5-10 minutes), cool, then pound or blend to powder; blend groundnut, pepper and ginger into a smooth paste; mix the aya powder with the groundnut blend; add honey, knead into a ball, wrap in foil if storing whole; store in a container at room temperature; mould into small balls to serve.

NOTE THAT THIS IS DAKUWA AYA — the tiger nut version, not the standard groundnut dakuwa. Standard dakuwa, groundnut-based, could NOT be found from any citable named source and is therefore not published in this collection.

It is one of only TWO recipes in the entire northern set consulted that contains cloves. The other is Abi Olayiwola's peanut-powder yaji variant, which she herself flags as a deviation (NGA081). Given that the academic description of yaji treats clove as canonical, the near-absence of cloves from published northern recipes is a real pattern.

ON DAKUWA GENERALLY, from Kitchen Butterfly's Lagos Island snack guide: 'Groundnuts and other nuts ground into a meal and pressed into little balls that crumble and melt on the tongue, barely held together with whispers of sugar, chili powder.' That describes the groundnut version and gives no quantities.

A RELATED LEAD NOT RETRIEVED: Nigerian Food TV has a 'Tanfiri (Donkwa) Recipe'. Donkwa is a northern groundnut-and-grain snack closely related to dakuwa and was not on the original brief; it is flagged here as worth adding to a future Hausa snack section.
storage: 3 weeks at room temperature in an airtight container, wrapped.
reheating: Not applicable — eaten at room temperature.
healthBenefits: Tiger nut is very high in fibre and in resistant starch.
Groundnut adds plant protein and niacin.
Honey rather than refined sugar as the binder.
Ginger and cloves both have documented anti-inflammatory activity.
culturalNote: The north has a deep repertoire of dry sweet snacks — dakuwa, donkwa, alkaki, sisi pelebe — built around groundnut, tiger nut and grain, all of them designed to keep without refrigeration. Tiger nut is eaten fresh, dried, ground into dakuwa and pressed into the drink kunun aya, which is a good deal of use from one small tuber.
